Doxycycline (DOX)-Inducible Short Hairpin RNA (shRNA) Knockdown

shRNAs (shHK2–1: GGATGTGTGTGAACATGGAATTTCAA- GAGAATTCCATGTTCACACACATCC; shHK2–2: CTTCATGGA- TAAGCTACAAATTTCAAGAGAATTTGTAGCTTATCCATGAAG; shHK2–3: CCAAAGACATCTCAGACATTGTTCAAGAGA- CAATGTCTGAGATGTCTTTGG; shHK2–4: CCGTAACATTCT- CATCGATTTTTCAAGAGAAAATCGATGAGAATGTTACGG; shHK2–5: CACGATGAAATTGAACCTGGTTTCAAGAGAAC- CAGGTTCAATTTCATCGTG; shCtrl: TAGCGACTAAACACAT- CAATTCAAGAGATTGATGTGTTTAGTCGCTA) were used for DOXinducible knockdown as described (15).

CRISPR Cas9 HK2 and HK1 Knockout

HK2 gRNA (TGACCACATTGCCGAATGCC) and HK1 gRNA (AGATGTTGCCAACATTCGTA) were used for HK1 and HK2 knockout as described (16).

Colony Formation Assay

Cells (1,000/well) were seeded in 6-well plates in the presence or absence of DOX (25 ng/mL). Media were refreshed every 3 d. After 15–20 d, colonies were stained with 2% crystal violet (17).

Glucose Consumption and Lactate Production

Cells (3 · 105) were seeded in 6-well plates in triplicate. After 24 h, medium was refreshed. Media from a well with no cells was used as a control. After 24 h, 1 mL of medium from each sample was analyzed in the Bioproﬁle Analyzer (Nova Biomedical). Values were normalized to cell number and time interval.

Medium Metabolite Measurements

Metabolites were measured as described (15) after 24 h cell culture.

Subcutaneous Xenograft Tumor Growth

Cells (Hep3B, 5 · 106; H460, 1 · 106; CFPAC1, 2 · 106) were implanted subcutaneously in nu/nu mice (Jackson Laboratory). Tumor volume was assessed by Vernier caliper measurement (D · d2/2; D and d are longest and shortest tumor diameters). For DOX-induced HK2 knockdown studies, xenograft tumors were allowed to grow to 200 mm3. Mice were then randomly assigned to 2 groups treated with control or DOX diet (625 mg of DOX per kg diet).

Cell Proliferation

Cell growth was assessed with a 3-(4,5-dimethylthiazol-2-yl)- 2,5-diphenyltetrazolium bromide assay (18).

Tumor Glucose Consumption by 18F-FDG PET/CT

Animals without fasting were warmed on a heating pad for 30 min, anesthetized with 2% isoﬂurane in oxygen, and injected via tail vein with 3.7 MBq of clinical-grade 18F-FDG. Mice were maintained under anesthesia in a heated induction chamber during the 1-h biodistribution period before imaging. PET/CT scans were conducted on a G8 instrument (Soﬁe Biosciences) with a 600-s PET acquisition and maximum-likelihood expectation maximization reconstruction, with a 50-s CT acquisition and Feldkamp reconstruction. PET/CT images were coregistered, and tumor regions of interest were analyzed using AM- IDE software.

Statistical Analysis

The Student t test was used for statistical analysis, and P value was determined by Prism 5 (GraphPad Software). Differences were considered statistically signiﬁcant at a P value of less than 0.05. Differential expression analysis between HK11HK21 and HK1-negative (HK12) HK21 liver cancer cell lines was conducted using the limma R package (19).

Studies (10–13) were published before CRISPR Cas9 gene inactivation technology became widely used. As an orthogonal approach to examine the role of HK2 in HK11HK21 cancer cell growth, we used CRISPR Cas9 to knockout HK2 in H460, U87, CFPAC1, and PC3 cells (Supplemental Fig. 4A). ## DISCUSSION

Upregulated aerobic glycolysis (the Warburg Effect) has been exploited with clinical 18F-FDG PET imaging for tumor diagnosis;

for tumor prognosis; and for choice, evaluation, and modiﬁcation of therapeutic modalities. The most prominent hypotheses for the functions of cancer cell aerobic glycolysis are supply of energy, reducing equivalents, or glucose carbon to build intermediates to support cancer progression (21). However, most glycolytically consumed glucose carbon is converted in tumor cells to released lactic acid (22); carbon mass in cancer cells comes predominantly from imported amino acids (23). How the Warburg Effect beneﬁts cancer is still inconclusive (24).

Although most normal tissues do not express HK2 (2), HK2 is expressed by most cancers and contributes to the upregulation of cancer aerobic glycolysis. Previous HK2 shRNA knockdown studies in HK11HK21

cell lines from breast (10), lung (10), prostate (12), pancreatic (11), and brain (13) tumors reported HK2 knockdown inhibited cancer cell proliferation in culture and xenograft tumor progression and suggested HK2 as a potential global cancer therapeutic target. However, using both those same shHK2 sequences (11–14) and shHK2 sequences we designed that have greater efﬁ- cacy in reducing HK2 levels, we did not observe signiﬁcant differences in cell proliferation, colony formation, or xenograft tumor growth in these cancer cells when HK2 expression was silenced, despite substantial differences in glucose consumption.

Using an orthogonal approach, we generated isogenic HK11HK2KO clones using CRISPR Cas9 technology and did not observe signiﬁcant effects on colony formation, cell culture proliferation, or xenograft tumor progression. However, glucose consumption in cell culture and small-animal PET imaging of 18F- FDG accumulation in vivo were similarly reduced, suggesting that HK2 is redundant in cancer cells that express high levels of HK1; HK11HK21 tumor cells have an excess, unneeded capacity for aerobic glycolysis; and although a useful tool for noninvasive measurements of tumor pharmacodynamics of HK2 inhibitors, 18F-FDG PET imaging would have limitations in predicting therapeutic outcomes of HK2 inhibitors in HK11HK21 tumors.

Our observations are consistent with a study that identiﬁed genes essential for cancer cell growth or survival in HK11HK21

human CML KBM7 cells using a genomewide screen (25). Neither HK1 nor HK2 was identiﬁed as an essential gene, suggesting their redundancy in cells that express both hexokinases. In contrast, HK2 is an essential gene in Jiyoye cells, a lymphoma cell line that expresses only low levels of HK1 (25). We conclude that, in cancers in which both HK1 and HK2 are expressed, HK1 and HK2 can compensate each other for cell proliferation and tumor progression. Consequently, targeting HK2 would not be an effective therapy in HK11HK21 cancers.

In examining the CCLE collection, we ﬁnd a signiﬁcant subset (6%) of cancer cells do not express HK1, with particularly high frequencies in multiple myelomas and liver cancers. No HK-targeted therapies have entered clinical cancer treatment, largely due to lack of selective HK2 inhibitors and lack of identiﬁcation of cancer types most sensitive to HK2 blockade. Molecular metabolic characterization of HK isoform expression, rather than tissue of origin, will guide the potential use of HK2- targeted cancer therapy for HK12HK21 cancers. We suggest that selective pharmacologic HK2 inhibitors will be promising agents for management of HK12HK21 cancers. However, our data also suggest that monotherapy with selective HK2 inhibitors will not eradicate HK12HK21 cancers; these cancers are likely to use other sources, for example, oxidative phosphorylation, for energy production to maintain survival. Combining agents targeting these other energy generation sources with HK2 inhibition, as precision therapies, may achieve synthetic lethality in HK12HK21 cancers and be tolerated by normal tissues that express HK1. Stratiﬁcation of patients with HK12HK21 cancers, particularly in multiple myeloma and liver cancer, would identify individuals for synergistic combination therapies involving selective HK2 inhibitors.

## CONCLUSION

Our data suggest a potential discrepancy between tumor 18F- FDG PET signal and tumor progression in HK11HK21 versus HK12HK21 tumors. Although therapeutic HK21 inhibition is likely to be restricted to HK12HK21 tumor subsets, stratiﬁcation of tumors of many different origins that express HK2, but not HK1, should identify tumors targetable with emerging selective HK2 inhibitors.

# Hyperinnervation Inhibits Organ-Level Regeneration in Mammalian Skin

**Authors:** Hannah T. Tam; Jingyu Peng; Rebecca Freeman; Yulia Shwartz; Shlomi Brielle; Sakshi Garg; Siti Rahmayanti; Stephen J. Crocker; Devin Coon; Ya-Chieh Hsu

## Abstract

Some mammalian tissues can replace lost cells within one lineage, but organ-level regeneration—restoring diverse cell types across lineages—remains rare. Here we show that late embryonic full-thickness skin injuries heal by regenerating epithelial, mesenchymal, neuronal, and vascular tissues with proper connectivity. However, this ability is lost soon after birth, leading to a failure to restore most cell types and hyperinnervation within the wound bed. Single-cell sequencing identified a postnatal wound-specific fibroblast (PWF) population absent after embryonic wounding. Through an in vivo screen, we discovered that three PWF-enriched genes—Timp1, Cxcl12, and Ccl7—inhibit organ-level regeneration and cause hyperinnervation when overexpressed in embryonic wounds. Reducing hyperinnervation in postnatal wounds through depleting Cxcl12 in fibroblasts or nerve ablation enables regeneration of diverse lineages after injury. Our study identifies mechanisms transitioning an organ from regenerative to non-regenerative, discovers fibroblast-driven hyperinnervation as a key barrier, and demonstrates removing this barrier unlocks organ-level regeneration.

## Abstract

Embryonic skin wounds regenerate diverse cell types across all lineages, but this capacity is lost soon after birth as a postnatal wound-specific fibroblast population drives excessive innervation that blocks regeneration. Reducing hyperinnervation at the injury site restores regenerative potential across lineages after postnatal wounding.

## Abstract

## INTRODUCTION

Organisms display a wide range of regenerative abilities. Planaria, hydra, and acoels can reform the whole organism from a small body fragment. Axolotls and zebrafish can regenerate organs composed of multiple lineages, including amputated limbs or fins and lesioned brains or spinal cords. In mammals, organ-level, multilineage regeneration is largely limited to the regeneration of digit tips, with a few special examples such as deer antlers, reindeer velvet, and several organs in spiny mice.1–13 Although mammals contain somatic stem cells that enable homeostatic cell replacement and tissue-level repair within individual lineages (such as epidermis, hair follicle, intestinal epithelium, and hematopoietic system), regeneration of a complex organ composed of many tissues from different lineages is rare.14–17 Even within mammalian organs that contain highly regenerative tissues, other tissues in the same organ often lack regenerative capacity or become dysregulated after injury. Skin is one such example.

Mammalian skin serves as a barrier against insult, infection, UV radiation, and dehydration. It also regulates body temperature and enables complex sensations. These multifaceted functions are mediated by a rich array of cell types from diverse lineages, including epidermis, hair follicles, melanocytes, immune cells, diverse innervation, blood vessels, lymphatic vessels, adipocytes, and fibroblasts.14,18,19 After a full-thickness injury, although the wound is closed by re-epithelialization of the epidermis, most other cell types fail to reform. In addition, some cell types, such as fibroblasts, react aberrantly to form scars—excessive, rigid collagen bundles arranged abnormally. Together, these changes compromise the skin’s ability to sense, regulate, and protect.

Nevertheless, previous studies have shown that under certain conditions, cell types other than the epidermis can regenerate to varying degrees after wounding. For example, in large wounds, some hair follicles and adipocytes can form in the center of the wound.20–23 In addition, activating SHH signaling or overexpressing LEF1 in the dermis leads to hair follicle induction after wounding.24,25 These findings suggest that cell types that typically do not regenerate after wounding might be able to do so when given inductive signals or when inhibitory blocks are removed. However, regeneration in these models remains incomplete, and whether additional skin cell types can regenerate and re-establish proper cross-lineage interactions remains largely unexplored, underscoring the need to better understand what enables multilineage regeneration.

Several mammalian cell types also display greater regenerative capacity or respond differently to insults early in life. For example, neonatal mice can regenerate cardiomyocytes, spinal cord axons, and hair follicles after injury, but this capacity declines rapidly with development.26–28 Conversely, the tendency to form scars increases with development.29 In the skin, while scar formation is prominent after postnatal injuries, embryonic fibroblasts do not produce excessive collagen and extracellular matrix when wounded and therefore heal without scar.30–32 Although scarless healing refers only to the absence of scar and is not synonymous with regeneration, structures reminiscent of early hair placodes have been reported after embryonic injury33,34, making it particularly interesting to explore whether other skin cell types can also regenerate to restore organ-level function during early development.

Inspired by these discoveries, we seek to understand—and expand—mammalian regeneration from the tissue level (replacing lost cells within one lineage) to the organ level (restoring diverse cell types across multiple lineages). Skin, with its diverse tissues across epithelial, mesenchymal, neural crest, and vascular lineages, serves as a prime model for this exploration. Is there a developmental window during which the skin can regenerate across multiple lineages with proper organization after injury? If so, when is this ability lost? What drives this differential regenerative capacity as development proceeds? Can we harness these principles to rebuild a multilineage organ after injury? Here, we address these questions using molecular, cellular, and tissue-level analyses of wound healing across development, coupled with an in vivo screen to uncover regulators of regeneration. In doing so, we discover that the skin initially possesses a remarkable capacity for organ-level regeneration that becomes progressively blocked with development, rather than irreversibly lost. By identifying these regeneration blockers, we establish a path to unlock its latent regenerative potential after injury.

## RESULTS

### Late embryonic skin wounds heal through regeneration of cell types across lineages

To assess the regenerative capacity of diverse skin cell types at different developmental stages, we created full-thickness wounds at embryonic day 16.5 (E16.5) and postnatal days 0, 2, 5, and 24 (P0, P2, P5, and P24) and examined wound healing outcomes. When skin was wounded at E16.5, cell types across lineages—including hair follicles, arrector pili muscles (APMs), lymphatic vessels and capillaries, melanocytes, sensory and sympathetic innervation, and dermal adipocytes—were readily detected in the wounded region and began to resume a morphology and organization similar to unwounded skin at 7 days after wounding. The regenerative ability decreased progressively at P0, P2, P5, and P24 (Figures 1A-C). When the skin was wounded at P5, re-epithelialization was completed, and fibroblasts refilled the dermis within 7 days. However, most other cell types failed to regenerate, accompanied by hyperinnervation in the wounded dermal region, increased myeloid cell infiltration, and hyper-thickened epidermis (Figures 1A, 1D, and S1A). Neither re-epithelialization nor dermal restoration was completed by 7 days after wounding at P24 (Figure 1B). Masson Trichrome staining confirmed that collagen in the healed P5 dermis was arranged in bundles parallel to the skin surface, a key feature of scar tissue in skin. By contrast, collagen in healed embryonic wounds was arranged in a non-parallel “basket-weave” orientation, similar to an unwounded wild-type skin, consistent with previous findings that embryonic wounds heal without forming scars (Figure S1B).30,33,34 In addition, scar-related myofibroblasts (α-smooth muscle actin-positive, or α-SMA+ fibroblasts) were observed 7 days after wounding at P5 but not after wounding at E16.5 (Figure S1C). As E16.5 and P5 are the closest two wounding timepoints that showed the most drastic differences in multilineage regeneration ability, we focused on these two timepoints for subsequent studies.

Time-course analyses revealed distinct healing processes following embryonic versus postnatal wounding. After E16.5 wounding, the epidermis became hyper-thickened at day 1 and day 2 post-wounding but resolved by day 3. Fibroblasts began migrating into the wound bed at day 2 post-wounding. Re-epithelialization was completed by day 3 post-wounding, where new placode- and hair germ–like structures formed from the newly closed epidermis (Figures S1D-F). By day 5, other lineages—including APMs, lymphatic vessels, melanocytes, and adipocytes—started to reappear, and innervation began to extend into the epidermis and regenerating hair follicles (Figure S1G). By day 7, the regenerated cell types in the wound appeared more developed than at day 5. Myeloid cells infiltrated the wounded region at day 1 but subsided afterwards. Adjacent unwounded skin contained more mature hair follicles, APMs, adipocytes, melanocytes, and innervation than the regenerating area (Figures 1C and S1D-G).

After wounding at P5, the wound bed was initially covered by a scab infiltrated with myeloid cells. Re-epithelialization, fibroblast migration, and innervation into the wound bed began around day 3. By day 6, re-epithelialization was complete. However, the wounded area exhibited dense dermal innervation and persistent, heightened myeloid cell infiltration, with no clear evidence of new hair placode formation (Figures S1H and S1I). Together, these findings demonstrate that embryonic wounds regenerate multiple skin cell lineages de novo, whereas postnatal wounds undergo repair characterized by scarring, heightened myeloid cell infiltration, and hyperinnervation.

### Regeneration is impaired, not delayed, after P5 wounding

Next, we examined whether regeneration following P5 wounding was merely delayed compared to embryonic wounding by assessing the skin 50 days post-wounding. Full-thickness skin wounds heal concentrically, causing nearby hair follicles to orient radially instead of along the anterior-posterior axis as in normal skin. In addition, hair follicles near the wound tend to grow longer and extend into the wound bed, confounding the distinction between regenerated structures and those from unwounded skin in cross-sections, especially long after wound closure. To address this challenge, we developed a wholemount 3D immunofluorescence imaging procedure that captures the entire wound together with the surrounding unwounded areas (Figures S2A-C). To help identify the wounded region in later analyses, we also injected fluorescent beads into embryonic wounds at the time of injury, in addition to marking the wounded area with henna ink (Figures S2D and S2E). Wholemount imaging confirmed that wounding at E16.5 led to robust regeneration across diverse lineages, restoring multiple tissues to a state closely resembling uninjured skin (Figures 2A and 2B). Sensory innervation re-formed delicate lanceolate ending important for perceiving gentle touch.35,36 APMs, sympathetic innervation, and lymphatic capillaries reconnected with hair follicle stem cells in a polarized manner.37–41 Adipocytes formed at the lower dermis.42–45 Melanocyte stem cells resided in the hair germ.46,47 The regenerated region restored all three major hair types in ratios similar to unwounded skin, including guard and awl/auchene hairs specified before E16.5 (Figures S2F and S2G). By contrast, many cell types remained largely absent 50 days after wounding at P5. Only sparse and immature hair follicles appeared occasionally. The healed area remained hyperinnervated and melanocytes were found in the dermis or epidermis where they are normally absent (Figures 2A and 2B). SMA+ myofibroblasts had disappeared by this time, consistent with previous findings that they represent a transient population after wounding.48 Together, these data suggest that by P5 the skin exhibits a loss in its ability to regenerate most cell types after wounding rather than a delay.

### Cell types regenerated after wounding at E16.5 are functionally interconnected

Because regeneration after wounding at E16.5 was nearly complete, we next asked whether these regenerated cell types resume proper connections and function, particularly those that require coordination across lineages. In response to cold temperatures, the skin forms goosebumps (piloerection) through concerted action of sympathetic nerves (neuronal), arrector pili muscles (mesenchymal), and hair follicles (epithelial).40 Therefore, for goosebumps to form in previously wounded regions, these three cell types must fully regenerate, reconnect in the correct position, and coordinate their actions in response to cold-induced sensory neuronal input. We found that healed E16.5 wounds regenerated all components of this tri-lineage unit with accurate connectivity: the APM connects to the lower bulge region of the hair follicle, and sympathetic innervation wraps around the APM to access the bulge. Moreover, upon cold exposure, the regenerated region exhibited classic goosebump reactions (Figures 2C and 2D). Taken together, these data suggest that E16.5 wound regeneration provides a model for studying organ-level, multilineage regeneration, with diverse cell types restored and connected in a manner that closely resembles uninjured skin morphologically and functionally.

### Distinct cellular and molecular changes in embryonic vs. postnatal wound healing

Next, we sought to identify key drivers of the distinct regenerative responses at E16.5 versus P5. To distinguish between the influence of the uterine environment and stage-specific changes in the skin, we manually delivered wounded embryos early at E18, allowing only the first 1.5 days of healing to occur in utero. Early delivery did not affect multilineage regeneration (Figure S2H). Together with the observation that P0 wounds still regenerate, albeit less completely than E16.5 wounds (Figure 1B), this suggests that the uterine environment is unlikely to be a major driver. Instead, stage-specific genes or cell types are more likely responsible. To identify these potential drivers, we performed scRNAseq on E16.5 wounded, P5 wounded, and unwounded age-matched control skin (2 biological replicates each). We sequenced wounds 3 days after injury to capture early changes that precede and may drive the distinct outcomes observed at later timepoints. To collect wound-responsive cells, we used a circular punch biopsy 1 mm larger than the wound to capture cells adjacent to and within the wound bed. After quality control, we obtained 94,779 cells for downstream analysis (Figure 3A). We performed unsupervised clustering, visualized the data using uniform manifold approximation and projection (UMAP), assigned cell identities based on differential gene expression, and grouped clusters into four major classes (Figures 3B and S3A): epithelial cells (7 populations), fibroblasts (13 populations), immune cells (8 populations), and others (muscle cells, endothelial cells, lymphatic vessels, Schwann cells, and melanocytes). Biological replicates showed strong overlap, and we recovered all known cell types (Figures S3B–D). These results show that, despite the limited tissue available at early stages of wound healing, we can successfully capture and profile diverse populations involved in both embryonic and postnatal wound healing with high quality.

At 3 days post-wounding, genes associated with hair placode formation (Sox9, Nfatc1, Lhx2, Gli1, Ptch1) were significantly upregulated in the epidermis of E16.5-wounded skin but not in P5-wounded skin. In contrast, P5 wounds upregulated injury-sensing, hypoxia, and tissue-repair genes (Stat3, Hif1a)49,50, as well as genes linked to proliferation (Mki67, Ccnd2) and migration (Rac1, Tmsb4x), consistent with reported roles of these genes in postnatal wound closure (Figure S3E).49–53

To further uncover mechanisms underlying the distinct regenerative outcomes, we asked whether embryonic and postnatal wounds differ in the presence or abundance of specific cell populations—either distinct cell types or transcriptional states. After P5 wounding, three populations stood out: (1) a significant increase in neutrophils, (2) a significant increase in a macrophage population (Mφ4), and (3) a fibroblast population that was absent in embryonic wounds and unwounded controls at both timepoints, which we named postnatal wound–specific fibroblasts (PWFs). By contrast, embryonic wounding did not result in distinct populations (Figure 3C). Flow cytometry confirmed a significant increase in myeloid cells 3 days after postnatal wounding but not after embryonic wounding (Figure 3D). Moreover, macrophage and neutrophil populations enriched in postnatal wounds displayed inflammatory features, including expression of pro-inflammatory cytokines (Il1a, Il1b, Tnf), chemokines (Cxcl1, Cxcl2, Cxcl3, Cxcl16), and the inflammasome gene Nlrp3, suggesting these cells promote and sustain inflammatory responses after wounding. Interestingly, postnatal wound-specific macrophages also expressed genes typically found in pro-repair macrophages54,55, including Arg1, Trem2, and Spp1, indicating that they may be at a transitional point shifting from an inflammatory state to a repair phase (Figure S3F). Neutrophils and macrophages clear bacteria and cellular debris, so these changes may partly reflect a stronger innate immune response after postnatal injury.

One of the most striking differences between embryonic and postnatal wounds is the emergence of PWFs, which are only present after wounding at P5 and absent after wounding at E16.5 and in unwounded controls. They are abundant after wounding at P5, comprising ~60% of all fibroblasts after postnatal wounding (Figures 3E and 3F). Immunofluorescence and RNAscope analyses confirmed that PWF-enriched genes (Timp1, Cxcl12) were preferentially upregulated in fibroblasts migrating into the wound bed after wounding at P5 (Figure S3G). Correlation and RNA velocity analyses suggested that PWFs predominantly arise from the lower fibroblast lineage, most likely from hypodermal fibroblasts (Figures S3H and S3I).56 PWFs are not enriched for En1, Taz, Yap1, or their transcriptional targets, and are overall transcriptionally distinct from the En1+ fibroblast population (Figures S3J-L).57,58 Additionally, only ~29% PWFs have myofibroblast characteristics (Acta2, Postn), suggesting that PWFs are composed of more than myofibroblasts (Figure S3M). To better understand the potential function of PWFs, we performed Gene Ontology (GO) enrichment analysis.59 GO term analysis suggested that PWF-enriched genes regulate diverse processes, including cell migration, collagen fibril organization, response to stress, angiogenesis, axon guidance, and inflammatory response (Figure 3G). These findings further highlight the potentially diverse role of PWFs in orchestrating multiple postnatal wound-specific processes.

### Establishment of an AAV-based approach to assess gene function in embryonic wounds

Because PWFs appear only after postnatal wounding, genes enriched in PWFs may inhibit multilineage regeneration. To test this possibility and identify specific genes that might inhibit regeneration, we sought to develop strategies to rapidly test gene function at scale in vivo during wound healing. We compared two different viruses—lentiviruses and adeno-associated viruses (AAVs, specifically AAV8)—by packaging a fluorescent protein (H2BGFP or tdTomato) under a constitutively active promoter (PGK or CAG) into each virus. We then simultaneously wounded the E16.5 skin and microinjected these viruses into the wounded region in utero. While both viruses effectively transduced embryonic wounds without affecting regeneration, lentiviruses induced a substantial immune response when introduced into the wound compared to AAVs, which may confound analyses (Figures S4A-C). We therefore selected AAVs as a vehicle for further optimization.

We first tested different titers of AAVs and found that ~1 × 1010 gc of AAVs robustly transduced embryonic skin (Figure S4C). Immunofluorescence and flow cytometry showed that tdTomato signals were detected within and immediately adjacent to the wound, but were largely restricted to dermal fibroblasts (Figures S4D and S4E). This finding was further validated in Pdgfra-H2BGFP mice transduced with AAV-CAG-H2BmCherry, where H2BmCherry-labeled nuclei colocalized with fibroblast nuclei (Figure S4F). To further assess which cell types were transduced by AAV, we FACS-purified tdTomato-positive and -negative cells 3 days after E16.5 wounding and AAV transduction and performed scRNAseq (2 biological replicates each). The results confirmed that the majority of AAV-positive cells were fibroblasts, encompassing nearly all dermal fibroblast cell types (Figures S4G and S4H). scRNAseq revealed no overt changes in cellular composition following AAV transduction (Figures S4I). Moreover, AAV-transduced embryonic wounds healed and regenerated comparably to non-transduced wounds, with no detectable changes in proliferation or apoptosis (Figures S4J and S4K). Altogether, these results establish AAVs as effective tools for testing gene functions in embryonic wounds.

### Selection of candidate genes

We next aimed to identify genes that could influence multilineage regeneration after embryonic wounding. Our analyses revealed that PWFs are enriched for secreted factors, which are of particular interest because of their potential to interact with diverse cell types and disrupt regenerative processes (Figure 3H). Given the non-cell autonomous and context-dependent nature of secreted factors, we reasoned that a phenotypic screen, although laborious, offered the best opportunity to identify PWF-enriched genes that functionally block organ-level regeneration.

To select candidate genes, we identified secreted factors enriched in PWFs relative to other skin populations and cross-compared them with several additional datasets: (1) genes more highly expressed in human adult fibroblasts compared to embryonic fibroblasts60, (2) genes elevated in reindeer backskin wounds, which do not regenerate hair follicles, compared to antler wounds, which do12, and (3) genes more highly expressed in scar-forming human skin wounds compared to scar-free oral mucosal wounds.61 From these comparisons, we narrowed the list to 9 PWF-enriched secreted factors that were also differentially expressed in at least one of these datasets (Figure 4A). These genes are predicted to function as chemokines (Ccl7, Ccl8, Cxcl12, Spp1), extracellular matrix modulators (Mmp19, Timp1, Crispld2), or secreted enzymes and chaperones (Sod3, Clu). However, whether and how they block regeneration remain unknown.

### An in vivo phenotypic screen identifies key genes that inhibit organ-level regeneration

To determine if any of these 9 genes inhibit regeneration, we individually overexpressed each gene using AAV delivery into E16.5 wounds (Figure 4A). Six genes tested did not disrupt regeneration when ectopically expressed during the embryonic wound healing (Figure S5A). However, overexpression of Ccl7, Cxcl12, or Timp1 disrupted regeneration after embryonic wounding—hair follicles, APMs, sympathetic innervation, lymphatic capillaries, melanocytes in the hair germ, and dermal adipocytes were all absent in the healed wound bed (Figures 4B, S5B, and S5C), suggesting that these three PWF-enriched genes can functionally block regeneration across diverse lineages.

We also observed interesting differences among these three regeneration-inhibitory genes: overexpression of Ccl7 or Cxcl12 in embryonic wounds resulted in significant hyper-thickening of the wound epidermis, a phenotype typically observed after P5 but not E16.5 wounding. By contrast, Timp1 overexpression resulted in only mild changes in epidermal thickness (Figures 4B and 4C). However, Timp1 overexpression increased myeloid cell infiltration into the wound bed, similar to that observed after P5 but not after E16.5 wounding. Surprisingly, overexpression of Ccl7 or Cxcl12 did not lead to significant changes in myeloid cell numbers, despite their presumed roles as chemokines (Figures 4C and 4D). Overexpression of each of these three genes induced hyperinnervation in E16.5 wounds by day 3, which became even more pronounced by day 7—a phenotype typically seen only after P5 wounding. Cxcl12 overexpression in particular further increased nerve fiber density and arborization (Figures 4C, 4E, S5D, and S5E). Taken together, our in vivo screen identified three genes that blocked organ-level regeneration after embryonic wounding, all of which led to hyperinnervation but differed in their effects on epidermal hyper-thickening and myeloid cell infiltration.

### Hyperinnervation but not myeloid cell infiltration inhibits regeneration

Our results thus far suggest that secreted factors enriched in PWFs not only inhibit multilineage regeneration but also induce postnatal wound-specific changes, including increased myeloid cell infiltration or hyperinnervation. These results prompted us to test whether changes in myeloid cells or innervation may affect regeneration outcomes (Figure 5A). We first tested if increased immune cell infiltration blocks regeneration. For this, we introduced lipopolysaccharides (LPS), key outer membrane components of gram-negative bacteria, into the amniotic sac and performed E16.5 wounding. Introducing LPS to the uterine environment significantly increased myeloid infiltration into the embryonic wound, yet multilineage regeneration persisted after E16.5 wounding (Figures 5B and 5C). To further assess whether changes in the immune landscape can alter regeneration outcomes, we used AAVs to overexpress additional cytokines. We selected Cxcl5, a cytokine enriched in PWFs, and Csf2, a potent cytokine that recruits and modulates diverse immune populations but is not enriched in PWFs.62 Overexpression of Cxcl5 increased myeloid infiltration, particularly neutrophils and dendritic cells, whereas Csf2 overexpression led to an even more pronounced recruitment of diverse myeloid populations as well as T cells. Despite these robust immune changes, overexpression of either cytokine in embryonic wounds did not induce hyperinnervation, and multilineage regeneration proceeded normally (Figures 5D-F). These results suggest that elevated myeloid infiltration and conditions resembling the non-sterile postnatal environment do not block regeneration.

We next asked whether inducing hyperinnervation in the embryonic wound bed—a shared phenotype following overexpression of Timp1, Cxcl12, or Ccl7—could inhibit regeneration. Hyperinnervation is also seen in human wound beds (Figure 5G), where it has been associated with post-wound hypersensitivity63,64, but its potential role in limiting regeneration has not been explored. To test if hyperinnervation blocks regeneration, we used an AAV to overexpress Ngf, which encodes nerve growth factor, a classical neurotrophic factor, in E16.5 wounds. Ngf overexpression induced pronounced hyperinnervation in the wound bed and prevented multilineage regeneration following E16.5 wounding (Figures 5B and 5H). Altogether, these findings indicate that hyperinnervation in the wound bed—characteristic of postnatal but not embryonic wounds—can impede regeneration.

### Reducing hyperinnervation or blocking synaptic vesicle release enables multilineage regeneration postnatally

Next, we investigated whether reducing hyperinnervation or blocking neuronal activity in postnatal wounds could enhance multilineage regeneration. To this end, we tested two complementary strategies to manipulate nerves in the wound bed. First, we treated postnatal wounds with botulinum neurotoxin A (BoNT/A), a bacterial toxin that cleaves SNAP-25 and disrupts the SNARE complex essential for neuronal vesicle release.65,66 BoNT/A treatment also reduced hyperinnervation (Figure S6A). Second, we selectively ablated sensory neurons by injecting AAV into the wound bed of VGlut2cre mice (Cre active in sensory neurons).67,68 The virus carried a Cre-activated caspase-3 construct (ef1a-flex-taCasp3-TEVp) packaged in AAV-MaCPNS1, a serotype optimized for peripheral neuron targeting.69,70 In both cases, myeloid cell infiltration was not significantly altered, yet multilineage regeneration was restored after postnatal wounding (Figures 6A-E and S6A-E). Together, these results suggest that reducing hyperinnervation or blocking neurotransmitter and neuropeptide release can effectively promote multilineage regeneration after postnatal full-thickness wounding.

### Fibroblast-derived CXCL12 drives hyperinnervation after postnatal wounding

Our data show that the hyperinnervation characteristic of postnatal wound healing inhibits multilineage regeneration. Because overexpression of Cxcl12, Ccl7, or Timp1 induces hyperinnervation in embryonic wounds, we next asked whether any of these genes directly recruit innervation into the wound site. We focused on Cxcl12 because its overexpression induced pronounced hyperinnervation with the most extensive nerve arborization (Figures 4C and 4E). Furthermore, qRT-PCR analysis showed that Cxcr4, its receptor, is more abundant in the dorsal root ganglion (DRG; sensory neuron cell bodies) at postnatal stages compared to embryonic stages (Figure S6F). To test if depleting Cxcl12 reduces hyperinnervation within the wound bed, we knocked out Cxcl12 from dermal fibroblasts using PdgfraCre; Cxcl12fl/fl (Cxcl12-cKO) mice and wounded these mice at P5 (Figure 7A). Loss of Cxcl12 from dermal fibroblasts significantly reduced hyperinnervation within the wound bed, while myeloid cell infiltration remained comparable to that of control postnatal wounds (Figures S6G-I). Consistent with this, scRNAseq analyses showed no major differences in immune cell populations or their transcriptional profiles between wounded controls and wounded Cxcl12-cKO mice at day 3 after wounding, indicating similarly elevated immune responses (Figures S6J and S6K). In addition, knocking out Cxcr4 in sensory neurons (VGlut2Cre; Cxcr4fl/fl, Cxcr4-cKO) reduced hyperinnervation after postnatal wounding without affecting myeloid cell infiltration (Figures S6L-N). Skin innervation was preserved in unwounded Cxcl12-cKO and Cxcr4-cKO mice, consistent with the idea that Cxcl12 upregulation in PWFs promotes innervation toward the wound bed (Figure S6O). Together, these findings suggest that CXCL12 attracts nerve fibers, not myeloid cells, to the wound bed, driving hyperinnervation seen after postnatal wounding.

### Knocking out Cxcl12 in fibroblasts enables multilineage regeneration after postnatal wounding

We next asked whether deleting Cxcl12 from fibroblasts could restore regeneration after postnatal wounding. Indeed, in Cxcl12-cKO mice wounded at P5, we observed robust regeneration of hair follicles, APMs, adipocytes, lymphatic capillaries, sensory and sympathetic nerves, and hair follicle melanocytes, with proper cross-lineage connectivity (Figures 7A-D). Although regeneration in wounded P5 Cxcl12-cKO mice proceeded more slowly than after embryonic wounding, it followed a similar sequence, with placode re-formation preceding other cell types. In control mice, innervation within the wound bed was evident by day 3 post-wounding and became even more prominent by days 5–6 after P5 wounding. In Cxcl12-cKO mice, placodes began to form around day 7 in the absence of hyperinnervation (Figures S1H, S1I, and S6P), consistent with the idea that hyperinnervation blocks regeneration that would otherwise occur in postnatal wounds. Similar multilineage regeneration was observed when Cxcr4 was deleted from sensory neurons, whereas no regeneration occurred when Cxcr4 was deleted from macrophages (the only other skin cell type expressing significant Cxcr4) or from keratinocytes (Figures 7A, 7E-G, S6Q, and S6R). Collectively, these findings demonstrate that fibroblast-derived Cxcl12 induces hyperinnervation, which prevents multilineage regeneration that would otherwise occur after wounding at early postnatal stages.

Lastly, we asked whether modulating Cxcl12 could enhance regenerative responses in adult skin. Cxcl12-cKO mice exhibited multilineage regeneration when wounded as adults, as did adult wounds treated with BoNT/A. Although regeneration was less extensive than in early postnatal skin, it was still significantly improved compared to wild-type adult wounds, which showed only re-epithelialization without regeneration of other cell types (Figures S7A-F). Regeneration in adults was further enhanced by simultaneously targeting all three genes identified in our screen—combining fibroblast-specific deletion of Cxcl12 and Timp1 with CCR2−/− mice, which lack one of the receptors for Ccl7 (triple-cKO mice) (Figures S7G-I). In these triple-cKO mice, hyperinnervation was significantly reduced after wounding, while myeloid cell infiltration remained high (Figures S6G-I). Altogether, our results identify hyperinnervation as a key barrier to multilineage regeneration, define its underlying molecular mediators, and highlight strategies to restore regenerative capacity in postnatal skin.

## DISCUSSION

The ultimate challenge in regenerative medicine is to regenerate all cell types across lineages to restore proper organ function after injury. While mammalian organs such as skin, gut, heart, or liver are often thought to be capable of regeneration under homeostatic or specific injury conditions, most current studies focus on tissue-level regeneration—that is, regeneration of a single tissue within these organs, such as the epithelial compartment of skin and gut, cardiomyocytes in the heart, or hepatocytes in the liver. Here, we study regeneration at the whole-organ level, considering cell types across epithelium, mesenchyme, neuronal lineage, neural crest lineage, and vasculature. By comparing organ-level regeneration following full-thickness skin injury at embryonic vs. postnatal stages, we show that skin rapidly transitions from regenerating a full array of cell types to failing to regenerate most of these cell types within eight days. We further identify hyperinnervation as a key barrier to organ-level regeneration.

Although Cxcl12 and Ccl7 are often viewed as chemokines that attract immune cells, their overexpression during E16.5 wounding did not alter the extent of myeloid cell infiltration. Moreover, experimentally increasing immune cell recruitment in utero—either by introducing LPS or by overexpressing Cxcl5 or Csf2—substantially elevated myeloid infiltration but did not disrupt organ-level regeneration following wounding at E16.5. In postnatal wounds, fibroblast-specific knockout of Cxcl12 likewise did not reduce the heightened myeloid infiltration, yet multilineage regeneration was restored. Together, these findings show that although immune cells play important roles throughout wound healing, and excessive inflammation can further worsen postnatal repair12,49,71–73, the extent of immune infiltration does not determine whether diverse cell types across lineages can reform after skin injury. Rather, the heightened immune responses after postnatal wounding likely reflect the need for host defense once the skin is exposed to the external environment.

CXCL12 is a versatile secreted factor involved in several regenerative contexts, with both anti-regenerative and pro-regenerative functions proposed.12,74–78 Most of its anti-regenerative effects are attributed to CXCL12’s role in immune cell recruitment, whereas the pro-regenerative effects are often linked to its regulation of angiogenesis. In this study, we provide evidence that CXCL12 promotes hyperinnervation in the wound. Although not a typical neurotrophic molecule, CXCL12 has been shown to influence motor neuron axon guidance and sprouting, suggesting that it may play a similar role in regulating sensory innervation after wounding.79

Sensory neurons reach the skin around E14.5 but continue to mature postnatally, with substantial increases in density and complexity.80–82 While complex sensory innervation endows organisms with rich and elaborate sensory experiences necessary for navigating the postnatal world, they are also prone to rapid and compensatory sprouting when severed.83–85 Although neurons play diverse roles in modulating tissue biology, regeneration, and immune responses39,40,66,86–95, these studies focus on mature innervation and often involve neuronal ablation across large regions or throughout the body. Much less is known about the nascent, densely sprouting sensory fibers that arise in the wound bed following nerve transection during wounding. Compared with mature nerve fibers, regenerating nascent axonal sprouts are hyperexcitable and prone to spontaneous firing, contributing to pain and hypersensitivity at the wound site. This heightened nociception alerts the organism and promotes pain-mediated avoidance behaviors that help prevent additional damage and support healing. However, these immature fibers can also release excessive neurotransmitters and neuropeptides that interfere with regenerative gene programs that would otherwise proceed. In addition, the sheer density of sprouting axons may physically impede the downgrowth of regenerating hair follicles and other dermal cell types, further limiting regeneration. In this sense, the intricate sensory network that matures postnatally comes at the cost of reduced multilineage regenerative capacity after wounding.

That said, our findings show that this trade-off is not fixed and can be shifted to favor regeneration. By blocking synaptic vesicle release or reducing hyperinnervation at the wound site, we enable multilineage regeneration after postnatal wounding. BoNT/A has shown promise in improving hypertrophic and keloid scars after their formation, although the mechanisms underlying its efficacy remain poorly understood.96–98 Our results suggest that applying BoNT/A during the early stages of wound healing—when regenerating axonal sprouts are abundant and multiple cell types may attempt to regenerate—might be even more beneficial. Because BoNT/A acts only for a limited period, local delivery can transiently dampen excessive neuronal activity in the wound bed, creating a window that permits regeneration without long-term sensory inhibition. In this sense, exchanging wound hypersensitivity and a brief, localized reduction in sensory function for substantially improved regeneration may represent a favorable and low-risk trade-off.

The loss of regenerative capacity with development is common across the animal kingdom.27,29,99–101 Our work suggests that, in some cases, the intrinsic ability to regenerate at the organ level may not be irreversibly lost, but rather blocked. We have shown that this block can be removed, either genetically or chemically, to improve multilineage regeneration in mammalian skin after injury. This work paves the way for treatments that promote more regenerative outcomes and restore greater functionality to the skin in chronic wounds or severe injuries. More broadly, it also establishes a framework for identifying and targeting similar regenerative blocks in other organ systems, thereby unlocking their latent regenerative potential.

### Limitations of the study

Our computational analyses suggest that PWFs are most likely derived from the lower fibroblast lineage, but definitive confirmation will require traditional lineage-tracing using appropriate CreER drivers. Whether CCL7 and TIMP1 directly attract nerves to the wound site or do so indirectly remains to be determined. Immune cells may also influence wound healing in processes not assessed here. Future work will be needed to determine whether embryonic-enriched genes, or additional cell types and mechanisms, also contribute to the divergent regenerative outcomes between embryonic and postnatal wounds. Defining the upstream regulation of PWF-genes lies beyond the scope of the current study but represents an interesting direction for future investigation.

## STAR★METHODS

### EXPERIMENTAL MODEL AND STUDY PARTICIPANT DETAILS

#### Animals

CD1 mice were obtained from Charles River Laboratories. C57BL6J, K14Cre, PdgfraCre, VGlut2Cre, Ccr2KO, Cxcr4fl/fl, and Cxcl12fl/fl mice were purchased from the Jackson Laboratory. CD64Cre mice were a gift from Ming Li and were provided to us by Ruth Franklin.102 Timp1fl/fl mice were described in Sutter et al.103 All experiments used a balanced number of male and female mice. For embryonic and postnatal wounding experiments, virgin adult females were time-mated with males. The presence of a copulatory plug in the morning was recorded as E0.5 for the embryos. All mice were maintained in an AAALAC-accredited (Association for Assessment and Accreditation of Laboratory Animal Care) animal facility at Harvard University. All procedures were approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee.

#### Human participants

Human wounding experiments were conducted with informed consent under Mass General Brigham Institutional Review Board approval (#2022P000229). Healthy adult female participants underwent standardized 5-mm punch biopsy wounding, and wound tissue was collected for downstream analyses as described in Method Details. Because only female participants were included, the influence of sex was not evaluated in this study.

### METHOD DETAILS

#### In utero embryonic skin wounding

Time-mated pregnant dams were anesthetized and provided with pre-operative analgesics. Hair on the abdominal skin was removed with depilatory cream and cleaned with povidone-iodine and alcohol wipes. A midline laparotomy on the abdomen was performed to minimally expose the uterine horn. The dorsum of embryos was positioned in view, and a purse string suture was passed through the uterine wall overlying the site of intended embryonic dorsal wounding while avoiding large blood vessels. A 2-mm incision through the uterine wall, amniotic sac, and embryonic skin was made at the center of the purse string suture. The incision site was rinsed with warm sterile 0.9% sodium chloride solution, then the purse string suture was tied closed. The intraperitoneal cavity and skin of the pregnant dam were sutured closed, post-operative analgesics were given, and the pregnant dam recovered under a heat source. Pregnant dams were provided with analgesics for the subsequent 2 days, monitored closely, and allowed to give birth and nurse naturally. For long-term tracking, wounds were marked using henna ink and microinjected with fluorescent beads.

#### Postnatal skin wounding

Neonatal mice were anesthetized with hypothermia, and adult mice were anesthetized with isoflurane. Dorsal skin was cleaned with povidone-iodine and alcohol wipes. A circular wound (3 mm for P0 and P2, 4 mm for P5, 6 mm for P24-P34 mice) was created at the center of the dorsal skin. After the procedure, the mice were allowed to recover under a heat source before returning to their nest. For long-term tracking, wounds were marked using henna ink.

#### Human skin wounding

Human wounding experiments were conducted under Mass General Brigham IRB #2022P000229. A 5 mm punch biopsy wound was created on the bilateral medial chest of study participants after injection of local anesthesia (lidocaine 1% with epinephrine). Wounds and surrounding skin margin were excised down to subcutaneous tissue and collected for analysis 13 days after wounding, followed by formalin fixation and paraffin embedding.

#### AAV and Lentivirus production and administration

pAAV-CAG-tdTomato was a gift from Edward Boyden (Addgene plasmid #59462) and was used as the control AAV plasmid. The following constructs were cloned into the same backbone: pAAV-CAG-Ccl7-t2A-EGFP, pAAV-CAG-Ccl8-t2A-EGFP, pAAV-CAG-Clu-3xHA, pAAV-CAG-Crispld2–3xHA, pAAV-CAG-Cxcl12-t2A-EGFP, pAAV-CAG-Mmp19–3xHA, pAAV-CAG-Ngf-t2A-EGFP, pAAV-CAG-Sod3-t2A-EGFP, pAAV-CAG-Spp1-t2A-EGFP, and pAAV-CAG-Timp1-t2A-mRFP. H2B-mCherry was a gift from Robert Benezra (Addgene plasmid #20972104) and was used to generate pAAV-CAG-H2BmCherry. These constructs were subsequently packaged with AAV8 capsids. pAAV-flex-taCasp3-TEVp was a gift from Nirao Shah and Jim Wells (Addgene plasmid #45580).70 These constructs were subsequently packaged with AAVMaCPNS1 capsids.69 pLV-GFP was a gift from Elaine Fuchs (Addgene plasmid #25999105) and was used to generate lentiviruses expressing H2BGFP (Boston Children’s Hospital). All plasmids were verified with whole plasmid sequencing before downstream applications. Virus titers were verified by quantitative real-time PCR of WPRE. All viruses that were intradermally injected into E16.5 skin were injected immediately prior to wounding (1 × 107 gc- 1 × 1010 gc). AAV-Casp3 was intradermally injected into P2 skin (1 × 1010 gc- 2.5 × 1010 gc).

#### LPS in utero administration

LPS was reconstituted with 0.9% sodium chloride solution at 0.5 mg/mL. A 2-mm incision was made through the uterine wall and amniotic sac, and 1 μL of LPS was pipetted into the uterine environment immediately before embryonic wounding. The incision site was closed with a purse string suture as described above.

#### Early-term delivery experiments

For early-term delivery experiments, embryos wounded at E16.5 were delivered at E18.0 via caesarean section. Wounded embryos were fostered by a lactating dam.

#### BoNT/A injection

BoNT/A (Abbvie) was reconstituted with 0.9% sodium chloride solution at 25 U/ mL. P4 or P21 mice were anesthetized and intradermally injected with 0.1–0.5 U of BoNT/A. The injection site was marked with henna ink to enable accurate identification for subsequent wounding the following day.

#### Piloerection experiments

Mice wounded on embryonic day 16.5 (E16.5) were used for piloerection experiments. To better visualize the effects of cold exposure on the regenerated wound area, the backskin was shaved except for the regenerated area. 50 days after wounding, mice were exposed to an ambient temperature of 4°C in a controlled environment chamber (Caron). Camera photographs were taken immediately after cold exposure to capture the instant hair-raising response.

#### Histology and immunohistochemistry

#### Section staining

Hair was removed by shaving prior to sample harvesting. Harvested samples were fixed using 4% paraformaldehyde (PFA) for 15 minutes at room temperature. Samples were washed with PBS, immersed in 30% sucrose overnight at 4°C, and embedded in optimal cutting temperature compound (Sakura Finetek). 50-μm sections were fixed again with 4% PFA for 2 minutes, washed with PBS, and blocked with blocking buffer (5% donkey serum, 1% BSA, 2% cold water fish gelatin in 0.3% Triton X-100 in PBS) for 1 hour at room temperature. Slides were stained with primary antibodies overnight at 4°C. Primary antibodies were washed off with 0.3% Triton X-100 in PBS, then slides were stained with secondary antibodies for 4 hours at room temperature. Secondary antibodies were then washed off similarly and the slides were mounted with Fluoromount-G® (SouthernBiotech).

For Masson Trichrome staining, samples were washed 6–8 times with PBS and immersed in 70% ethanol at 4°C overnight before paraffin embedding. 6-μm sections were stained with Masson Trichrome (Sigma-Aldrich) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. H&E stainings were performed according to the manufacturer’s instructions (Sigma-Aldrich). Fluorescent RNA in situ hybridization was carried out in fresh frozen 20-μm sections using the RNAscope® Multiplex Fluorescent Reagent Kit v2 (ACD Bio). Sections were fixed in 4% PFA for 1 hour at 4°C, followed by three washes with 0.1% Tween-20 in PBS. Samples were dehydrated through an ethanol gradient series and pre-treated with RNAscope hydrogen peroxide solution for 10 minutes at room temperature. The mm-Cxcl12 Probe (ACD Bio) mixture, Amp 1, Amp 2, and Amp 3 were applied sequentially at 40°C, with incubation times of 2 hours, 30 minutes, 30 minutes, and 15 minutes, respectively, and with two washes between each step. TSA Vivid Fluorophore 570 was applied for 30 minutes at 40°C and washed off. HRP activity was quenched using the RNAscope HRP blocker for 15 minutes at 40°C, followed by two washes. Samples were counterstained with DAPI and mounted with Fluoromount-G®.

For human wounds, samples were deparaffinized with xylene and rehydrated through an ethanol gradient series. Antigen retrieval was performed in boiling citric acid buffer (pH 6.0) for 15 minutes. Samples were washed two times with 0.1% Tween-20 in PBS, permeabilized with 0.5% Triton X-100 in PBS for 15 minutes, and washed two additional times with 0.1% Tween-20 in PBS. Samples were blocked with 5% donkey serum, 1% BSA, and 2% cold water fish gelatin in 0.3% Triton X-100 in PBS for 1 hour at room temperature. Primary antibodies were applied overnight at 4°C, followed by three washes with 0.1% Tween-20 in PBS. Secondary antibodies were applied for 1.5 hours at room temperature and washed three times with 0.1% Tween-20 in PBS. Samples were mounted with FluoroSave (Millipore).

#### Wholemount staining

Skin samples were fixed in 4% PFA for 1 hour at room temperature, washed with PBS, and immersed in 30% sucrose at 4°C overnight. The panniculus carnosus muscle was carefully removed with fine forceps. Samples were permeabilized in 0.3% Triton X-100 in PBS for 5 hours at room temperature and then blocked with 5% donkey serum, 1% BSA, and 2% cold water fish gelatin in 0.3% Triton X-100 in PBS for 2 hours. Primary antibodies were applied for 24 hours at room temperature, followed by 5 washes with 0.3% Triton X-100 in PBS. Secondary antibodies and DAPI were then applied for 24 hours at room temperature and washed in the same manner. Samples were refixed in 4% PFA for 1 hour at 4°C, washed with 0.1 M glycine in PBS for 30 minutes, and rinsed twice with 0.3% Triton X-100 in PBS for 30 minutes each. Samples were dehydrated in methanol and cleared with ethyl cinnamate before mounting on a 35 mm glass-bottomed microscope slide for analysis.

#### Imaging and image analysis

Samples were imaged using a Nikon CSU-W1 spinning disk confocal microscope (x4, x10, x20 objectives), Zeiss LSM 900 confocal microscope (x10, x20 objectives), or Keyence BZ-X710 widefield microscope (x10, x20 objectives). Images are presented as maximum intensity projection images or a single z-slice. Images were analyzed and rendered using ImageJ.106 To quantify wound epidermal thickness, the straight-line tool in ImageJ was used and positioned at a 90° angle perpendicular to the epidermis. For each biological replicate, three measurements were taken at different locations within the wound region and subsequently averaged. Immune cells in the wound bed were quantified by setting a 250 × 300 μm ROI and manually counting cells through a 50 μm z-stack using the ImageJ Cell Counter. Counts were converted to cells/mm2. To quantify innervation of the wound bed, the Imaris FilamentTracer tool was used. ROI(s) for each image were set according to the wound bed dimensions using DAPI, and filaments were identified using nerve (TUJ1) staining. The algorithm was manually trained to identify true nerve staining. Filament volumes and branches were normalized to VROI /1000 μm3.

#### Fluorescence-activated cell sorting (FACS)

Mouse dorsal skin was harvested, and 3–5-mm biopsy punch tools were used to dissect out the wounds. Wounds were treated with 0.25% collagenase in Hank’s Balanced Salt Solution for 22–40 minutes at 37°C on an orbital shaker. Wounds were scraped with a scalpel, and cells were collected and centrifuged at 400g for 10 minutes at 4°C. Cells were treated with 0.25% trypsin-EDTA for 10 minutes at 37°C and filtered through 70-μm and 40-μm filters. Samples were resuspended in 5% FBS in PBS and stained with fluorescent-conjugated antibodies for 30 minutes. The following antibodies were used: CD11b-FITC (eBioscience, 11–0112-82, 1:250), CD11b-PE-eFluor610 (eBioscience, 61–0112-80, 1:500), CD140A-PE-Cy7 (eBioscience 25–0311-81, 1:150), CD45-eFluor450 (eBioscience 48–0451-82, 1:250), CD64-PE-Cy7 (Biolegend, 138313, 1:250), and Ly6G-APC (Biolegend, 127613, 1:100). DAPI (Sigma-Aldrich, 0.1 ng/ mL) was used to gate out dead cells. FACS experiments were performed using BD FACSAria II+ sorters.

#### RNA isolation

DRGs were lysed directly into Trizol LS Reagent (Invitrogen). RNA was isolated using the RNeasy Micro Kit (Qiagen) and the QIAcube according to the manufacturer’s instructions. RNA concentrations were assessed with either Qubit or the Bioanalyzer and RNA 6000 Pico chip (Agilent). RNA integrity was assessed using the Bioanalyzer. Only samples with an RNA Integrity Number of 7 or higher were used for subsequent quantitative real-time PCR experiments.

#### Quantitative real-time PCR (qRT-PCR)

cDNA libraries were synthesized using Superscript IV Vilo master mix with ezDNase (Thermo Fisher). qRT-PCR was performed using SYBR Green (Thermo Fisher). CT values were normalized to β-actin.

#### Single-cell RNA-sequencing data generation and analysis

Single-cell suspensions were treated with ACK lysis buffer to remove red blood cells prior to FACS sorting. 16.5K live (DAPI negative) cells per sample were loaded into the 10X Genomics Chromium Next GEM Chip G. scRNAseq gene expression libraries were generated using the 10X Genomics Chromium Next GEM Single Cell Kit (v3.1) as per manufacturer’s protocol. Libraries were sequenced on a NovaSeq 6000 S4 lane.

The 10X Genomics cellranger pipeline (v7.1.0) was used to align reads to the GRCm38 - mm10 genome and to generate initial gene expression tables for individual barcodes. Gene-barcode matrices were imported into Seurat (v4.3,) for subsequent analyses in R (v4.2.3).107 Genes detected in <5 cells were excluded. Cells with a mitochondrial gene percentage >10% were removed, as were low-quality cells with fewer than 500 detected genes or putative doublets with more than 8000 genes. Log normalization was then applied using the NormalizeData function (scale.factor = 10000). Highly variable features were identified using the FindVariableFeatures function (method = vst). Principal component analysis was performed using the RunPCA function. The number of principle components used for follow-up analysis was determined with the ElbowPlot function. Unsupervised clustering was performed using the FindNeighbors and FindClusters functions (dims = 1:50, resolution = 0.4). Pearson correlation analyses were performed with the cor R function using averaged gene expression generated from the Seurat AggregateExpression function. The FindAllMarkers (using the Wilcox rank sum test) function was used for differential gene expression analyses. One cluster out of 36 identified clusters was removed from further analysis due to low cell number and UMI. Gene set enrichment analyses were performed using ShinyGO.59 Statistical significance was given to genes with false discovery rate (FDR) <0.05. The AAV dataset was projected onto the un-injected dataset using the IntegrateData function. Plots were generated using plotting functions in Seurat and ggplot2 (v3.4.3). Correlation analysis between cell types was performed using Pearson correlation of scaled, highly variable genes; one doublet-enriched population was excluded from correlation analysis. A dendrogram was generated by hierarchical clustering with average linkage to visualize relationships among cell types. For RNA velocity analysis on fibroblasts, spliced and unspliced transcript counts were generated using Velocyto.108 The resulting .loom files were processed in Python using scVelo.109 Within scVelo, data were normalized and log-transformed, moments were computed across nearest neighbors, and RNA velocities were estimated using the stochastic model. Velocity vectors were projected onto the UMAP embedding to visualize transcriptional dynamics and infer lineage relationships. Upregulated genes in PWFs compared to other cell types were considered significant using the Wilcoxon Rank Sum Test (pct >0.25 and logFC > 0.25). For comparison across multiple wound healing or regenerative contexts, we used previously published datasets for human fetal vs adult fibroblasts (logFC > 1, adjusted p-value < 0.01)60, human oral mucosa vs. cutaneous wound healing (day 3 and 6 after wounding, logFC > 1, adjusted p-value < 0.01)61, and reindeer antler velvet fibroblasts vs backskin fibroblasts (day 3 after wounding, logFC > 0.25, Wilcoxon rank-sum-determined two-sided p-value < 0.05).12

### QUANTIFICATION AND STATISTICAL ANALYSIS

Statistical analyses were performed with Prism (GraphPad) using unpaired two-tailed Student’s t test and one-way ANOVA with Tukey’s or Dunnet’s multiple comparisons test as appropriate. All statistical details (sample size, statistic methods, and P value) are provided in the figure legends. Statistical significance of differences in single pairwise comparisons was assessed using unpaired two-tailed t-test assuming Gaussian distribution with 95% confidence interval. Multiple group comparisons, with a single changing variable, were evaluated using one-way ANOVA. Tukey’s post-hoc test was used to evaluate pairwise comparison within ANOVA datasets when all groups were tested pairwise against all others, Dunnett’s test was used when multiple groups were compared to a single control. No statistical methods were used to predetermine sample size. Investigators were not blinded, as identification of specific genotypes and the distinct appearance of wounded mice made blinding not possible. One single-cell cluster was removed from further analyses due to low cell number and UMI. One doublet-enriched cluster was excluded from correlation analyses. No animals or other data were excluded. Data are represented as mean ± SD.
